speakeroldname: Mr. T. L. CHURCH (North Toronto) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government of Canada should give early and favourable consideration to the report of the International Joint Commission on the St. Lawrence River Waterway, and request the Government of the United States to join with Canada in making an international agreement for carrying out the work so recommended.
He said:	I offer no apologies for introducing this motion, which I had intended moving on Monday. The three parties in the House will agree, I think, that it is of sufficient importance to warrant not only an afternoon's discussion, but consideration on a second day as well. A debate on this very subject has been in progress in the United States Congress and Senate for some six weeks, and to-day the question I am bringing up in this resolution is the most important one that has been before the people of Canada since Confederation and the building of the Canadian Pacific railway. Not only is it of great concern to us in Canada, but it is one of the most important economic questions under consideration on the North American continent at the present time. I would point out that it is not and should not be made a political question at all; it is a business question, a great economic question, a transportation question that concerns every citizen both of the United States and of Canada. It should therefore be approached not from the provincial, the
St. Lawrence Waterway

local, parish, or sectional standpoint, but from the great national standpoint of what is the greatest good for the greatest number. This subject is so vast and intricate that it is almost impossible to do more than touch the fringe of it in the short time at my disposal this afternoon. It has supporters among all parties in Canada, in and out of the House.
We have three transcontinental railway systems, and in that respect we are far ahead of the economic development of the country. In fact, we could for some years probably get along with one or two such systems, and the money spent on the third could have been spent to much better advantage in deepening this waterway to the sea. Had we done this we would have acquired a gilt-edged security, and solved the transportation question, and from the standpoint of power alone the deepening of the St. Lawrence would have more than paid the cost incurred, to say nothing of saving millions of dollars in freight charges, and so effecting economies in transportation which would redound to the economic advantage of the whole country. And we would have provided a feeder for the National lines, and Canadian Pacific railways to the head of the Lakes and would have solved in the main the transportation problems of this country as well as of the United States.
A review of our canal policy does not disclose what might be called any deliberate, well planned or consistent policy. Money has been spent on some canals that should never have been undertaken; whereas if that money had been diverted to the deepening of the St. Lawrence channel and the Welland canal it would have provided a great national asset. The Welland canal deepening has been more or less a political football. This canal is an important link in the St. Lawrence scheme, and it should have been finished long ago. Indeed, if the work had been prosecuted with the same vigour that characterized the construction of the Chippawa-Queenston power canal, we would have that link in operation to-day. As it is, however, we are told that it may be 1927, and more probably 1937, before the canal is deepened. Until the Welland ship canal is completed a 500,000 bushel barge coming down from Port Arthur has to tranship its cargo of wheat at Port Colborne into smaller boats, at a cost of four cents a bushel, and there is the further disadvantage that most of that wheat goes to Buffalo instead of to Montreal.

With the opening of the new Welland ship canal boats will be able to run from Port Arthur direct to Montreal at a rate of about four or five cents a bushel to Port Colborne, and one cent to two cents for the extra run, Port Colborne to Montreal, without transhipment to smaller boats at Port Colborne, as now.
The St. Lawrence river waterway is being strongly supported by all the Western states,-Ohio, Illinois, Indiana, Wisconsin, Michigan, Iowa, Minnesota, the Dakotas, Nebraska, Colorado, Montana, Wyoming and Idaho. The legislatures of those states have for years been voting money for surveys, and for an educational campaign in connection with this important scheme. In Canada the governments of Ontario and Saskatchewan have come out very strongly in its favour. In addition, a thousand chambers of commerce and boards of trade and patriotic bodies in the two countries have passed resolutions in favour of it. The opposition to the project is centered in New York and in some parts of Quebec and Montreal. It should be observed, however, that those in Canada do not oppose the scheme from the economic or transportation standpoint, but because they favour some rival scheme. I am not going to decry those rival schemes, because I think that before many years are past we may need not only the St. Lawrence but the Georgian Bay waterway as well, in the same way as at one time one railway was sufficient for our transportation needs, and later with the development of the country a second and even a third railway system was constructed.
A notable utterance in favour of this waterway was delivered by President Harding at the agricultural conference at Washington on the 23rd January last, in the course of which he said:
I have spoken of the advantage which Europe enjoys because of its access to the sea, the cheapest and surest transportation facility. In our own country is presented one of the world's most attractive opportunities for extension of the sea-ways many hundred miles inland.
The heart of the continent, with its vast resources in both agriculture and industry, would be brought into communication with all the ocean routes by the execution of the St. Lawrence waterway project. To enable oceangoing vessels to have access to all the ports of the Great Lakes would have a most stimulating effect upon the industrial life of the continent's interior.
The feasibility of the project is unquestioned, and its cost, compared with some other great engineering works, would be small. Disorganized and prostrate, the nations of Central Europe are even now settling their hands to

St. Lawrence Waterway
the development of a great continental waterway which, connecting the Rhine and Danube, will bring water transportation from the Black to the North Sea, from the Mediterranean to the Baltic.
If nationalistic prejudices and economic difficulties can be overcome by Europe, they certainly should not be formidable obstacles to an achievement less expensive and giving promise of greater advantages to the peoples of North America. Not only would the cost of transportation be greatly reduced, but a vast population would be brought overnight in immediate touch with the markets of the entire world.
There you have the declaration of the President of. the United States. I hope, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. leader of the House (Mr. Mackenzie King) will, before this dehate is concluded, appoint another day for further discussion, as the subject is of such supreme importance that it is impossible to give it proper consideration in the short time at our disposal this afternoon. This is, perhaps, the most important question that this Parliament will have to settle, and full opportunity should be given for an exhaustive discussion of the merits and demerits-if there are any-of this great scheme, and of the report of the Deep Waterways Commission.
In connection with this subject it is relevant to refer briefly to the history of the St. Lawrence river and a few of its physical characteristics, and the artificial improvements made on the Lakes by Canada since 1809, in order that the importance of this waterway and its development may be properly appreciated.
The St. Lawrence rises in lake Ontario and discharges its waters into the gulf of St. Lawrence, but what one might term its primary source is at the head of the St. Louis river at the extreme end of lake Superior, 1,870 miles from the gulf. The basin of the St. Lawrence is a great transverse valley, 309,500 square miles in area, extending from the gulf of St. Lawrence into the heart of the continent. Much the larger part of the basin lies north of the boundary, as all its great tributaries flow in on that side. It is separated by a low divide from the Hudson bay basin, and from the Mississippi basin by an even lower divide. The river is remarkable for the number of expansions in its course.
Many surveys and charts have been made of this river since 1809, and a great deal of money has been expended on widening and deepening its channel since that time. The history of the St. Lawrence ship channel proper between Quebec and Montreal starts in 1825, when Hon. James Young,
of Montreal, an intensely patriotic man, interested the government in the matter, with the result that a great deal of early investigation, survey and educational work for improving the channel was carried out between 1836 and 1841. This work was made the subject of inquiry by a committee of the Lower Canada legislature, 1836 to 1841. Their report was published and the work was begun, continued and carried to completion by the Harbour Commission. The gentlemen composing that commission from time to time have done an immense amount of work in improving the St. Lawrence channel and harbour of Montreal, improvements involving heavy expenditures. But, as one of the harbour commissioners for Toronto, I am free to admit that money spent on any of our great harbours, such as Quebec, Halifax, St. John, Montreal, Toronto, Vancouver, and Victoria, enures to the advantage of the country generally, and should not be considered as purely a local improvement, because these ports are all a factor in the development of deep waterways and of water-borne traffic. When this important work was handed over by the government of Canada to the Montreal Harbour commissioners, the commissioners went ahead and did very good work. They appointed a board of engineers to inquire into the project. The matter was examined from all points of view and a report was brought down recomanending the improvement of the channel between Quebec and Montreal. That report of the engineers was adopted by the government and the Montreal Harbour Commission and operations were begun by the commission on the old channel in 1851. By November, 1851, this channel was opened to lake St. Peter to a depth of ten feet six inches. In 1853 a vessel passed through to the foot of lake St. Peter draw-four feet more than the ordinary depth of water. In 1855 the capacity was increased to sixteen and' one-half feet, and1 subsequently in 1857, to eighteen feet. In 1856 the harbour commissioners pointed out to the government the national character of the work which they had been doing, urging that the work had been for the government of Canada and that the money expended had been devoted to national purposes, for the advantage of the whole country. Outstanding success attended the early operations of the Harbour Commission of Montreal, and the channels were further deepened from time to time, until to-day there is a 35-foot channel 450 feet wide. Prom 1851 to 1888 the harbour com-
St. Lawrence Waterway

missioners had charge of this ship canal, but in 1888 the work was transferred back to the federal Department of Public Works. There it remained until 1904, when it was transferred by the government of the day to the Department of Marine and Fisheries. That is a short history of the St. Lawrence ship channel. The cost of the improvements to that channel to date, according to a return laid on the table of the House on March 20, 1921, has been $23,867,000.
No proper study of this question can be pursued without an understanding of the territory on both sides of the international border which is tributary to this work. The fourteen states I named' in the early part of my address, situated in the central and western parts of the United States, are all tributary to this work and will benefit by it, from the transportation as well as from the navigation, power and economic standpoint. The part of Canada most directly affected by this project as a national work are the entire province of Ontario and the parts of Manitoba and Saskatchewan south of the National Transcontinental. This territory on both sides of the border is the greatest industrial territory. The districts affected in Canada are noted for the production of grain, live stock and dairy products, and forest resources-not only in Ontario, but in other parts of Canada. Then, there is the value of the wood used for pulp manufacture; the value of mineral products, coal and copper deposits; and of manufactured goods generally. The freight traffic on the railway lines running through the territory tributary to this work amounts to 37,000,000 tons annually. I admit that the tributary territory in the United States is suffering to-day, in a railway sense, more than the tributary territory in Canada is, because in the United States they are away behind the times as shown by the congestion of railway traffic. In Canada we have no lack of mileage; we have three transcontinental railways. In fact, we have what I might call useless duplication and waste. But we have not the development of waterborne traffic, and in that respect our condition differs from that of the United States.
I wish to say a few words with regard to this question from the navigation standpoint as 'it affects the people of Canada and the people of the United States. Many phases of the question have been studied during the past fifty years from the point of view of navigation; I will enumerate only la few of them. One of the results

of this development will be the increase of production through improvement of the avenues of transportation and the creating of new ones. The history of waterborne traffic the world over makes it plain that when an important canal or waterway is improved, cheaper freight rates follow, with consequent increased production and closer co-operation between producer and consumer.
Another phase of the question bears upon the effect of improved transportation facilities for water-borne traffic upon the rail route. No less an authority than Mr. Hoover, one of the most eminent men in the United States to-day, gives it as his opinion that if adequate water-borne communications are provided they will act as feeders for the steam roads and have the effect of reducing and regulating rates. 1 believe that this important work would produce in Canada such revenue for our bankrupt railroads that in a few years they would become a gilt-edged investment. As to the effect upon the railroad congestion, we have the evidence of the new premier of Saskatchewan, Hon. Charles A. Dunning, who refers to the fact that in Canada at the present time there is not the acreage cultivated that there is in normal times, and that with the expansion of agriculture, the cultivation of a greater acreage and the production of a normal crop, there would be very serious railway congestion in the western parts of the country; the railways would not be able to take the crop out. We must provide a route for this water-borne traffic via the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence without transhipment, if we are to solve the congestion problem and problem of freight rates for East and West alike.
Another question arising from the navigation standpoint is, how will ocean rates and inland water rates be affected? The effect will be a saving of five or six cents a bushel on wheat carried from the head of the Lakes to the seaboard. I will not quote the facts bearing upon this point which were placed before the International Commission by some of the gentlemen who came from the West.
Then, there is the effect upon package freight taken from the head of the Lakes to the seaboard and from the seaboard to the head of the Lakes without transhipment. Mr. Richardson, of Kingston, a very prominent man in transportation circles, who has an office in Winnipeg, expresses the view that the development of package frieght transportation on the Lakes will revolutionize things for the

St. Lawrence Waterway
small cities and towns. The small freighter can proceed from Montreal up the river, stopping at Brockville, Kingston, Hamilton, Cobourg, passing through the Welland canal and proceeding to Port Colborne, Sarnia and Windsor and thence to the head of the Lakes. Hon. members would be surprised to see the small freighters coming into these lake ports as I have seen them and the boon they are to the public. They put down their package freight without delay; the merchants can have the goods in their retail stores the same day, and they know when they are going to get them. This project will revolutionize the package freight business on the Great Lakes; that is amply demonstrated by the number of package freighters operating on the Great Lakes to-day, notwithstanding the difficulties with which they have to contend.
What will be the relative cost of building and operating lake ships and ocean ships, and what are the characteristics of each? Some large ocean freighters to-day are not constructed for service on the Great Lakes, and vice versa. Many of the old type of boats, commonly known on the lakes as the whaleback, have already gone down the lakes to the Atlantic seaboard ports with freight. We have the evidence of many eminent men who have sailed the lakes for many years, that three-fourths of all the ocean boats in the world to-day do not draw more than twenty-five feet, and these boats could go to the head of the lakes if we adopt this scheme. I shall not take time to read their evidence because there are other speakers. Three-fourths of the ships that go through the Suez and Panama canals could use the lakes with this improvement.
I believe that if this project goes through, it would result in a great expansion of the shipbuilding industry on the Great Lakes, and that would do more to solve unemployment than any other agency that I know of. I believe that we can produce the right type of ships not only for the ocean but for the lakes as well. Salt water boats could then go up the St. Lawrence river one thousand miles, as every navigation man knows. The same is true of the Amazon river, where ocean ships go up 1,000 miles.
What will be the effect if it is practicable to build a composite type of vessel for lake and ocean use. It will stimulate shipbuilding on the lakes and there will be sufficient cargoes both inbound and outbound to keep the ships busy. It will be of the greatest economic value on both sides of the border.
The fact that this district is a great consumer, and the home of many of the greatest basic industries on the continent of America, will be enough to provide cargoes to the head of the lakes and to the seaboard.
Those who are opposed to this project talk of ice conditions and fog, but that would be no more an adverse factor than it is on the American seaboard part of the year. Of all the fogs you see, there are none worse than those that envelop the ports of the Atlantic and Belle Isle. So this project stands on an equal basis with the Atlantic seaboard in that respect. The St. Lawrence is all right for five to six months of the year as to climatic conditions.
There are many other features of this scheme that might be touched upon-the competition between lake freighters and ocean vessels, the necessity of cutting channels and deepening inland harbours. With respect to the latter, many inland harbours are to-day ten and fifteen years ahead of their work in anticipation of this project. Cleveland, Detroit, Toledo and Buffalo are deepening their harbours and the United States government are bringing on advance expenditures instead of curtailing expenditure for deeper harbours as we are doing on this side of the border for deeper harbours.
The United States Government are increasing grants for deepening ports and harbours and for providing deeper water in all the channels. They have just brought down a bill in Congress appropriating many millions for lake ports.
Toronto is spending $26,000,000 rebuilding its harbour. The city itself is putting up eighty-three per cent of the cost of all these improvements through its Harbour Board.
It is not a beautification scheme, but a great commercial, economic scheme to provide docks and do something to develop water-borne traffiee for the good of the country generally. I shall not refer any further to the navigation aspects of this project, except to say that it will be a very great factor in moving grain to the seaboard, and will obviate the losses that occur in transhipment at Port Colborne and Prescott, for instance, and prevent in the future a railway blockade and reduce heavy freight rates by rail.
Following the consummation of this work I believe Canada will experience an era of the greatest industrial expansion it has ever known. Alternative routes have been
St. Lawrence Waterway

proposed, but I shall not deal with them, as other speakers are to follow. I have always been a believer in the St. Lawrence route. It has long appealed to my fancy and imagination, and the more I study the proposition the more I am convinced that it is one of the greatest projects the people of Canada have ever had before them for good and the welfare of the country.
I want to refer to another aspect of this project, and it is one of the greatest questions before the people of Canada to-day- the question of water-power. The waterpower that would be developed incidentally in the building of this canal would more than pay for the cost of the work. It is only within the last two hundred years that scientific discoveries have given to the world the power inherent in fuels, namely, coal, oil, gas and falling water, distributed in the various forms of heat, light, and electricity. It has been estimated that the total water-powers of the world amount to about
100,000,000 horse-power, of which only about 17,000,000 have so far been developed. The Dominion of Canada possesses about twenty per cent of the world's total waterpower and also approximately the same percentage of the world's water-power already developed. The people of Ontario and Quebec are especially interested in this power situation. In Ontario we have no coal. We have to depend for our coal supply on the maritime provinces, or the far West and the United States. The United States will run out of coal in one hundred years, as has been shown by the report of the Conservation Commission of that country. The first of these stores of energy to be utilized by man was coal, as we all know. This fuel is very widely distributed and exists in immense quantities in various parts of the world, but there is no denying the fact that the supply is limited and the world is not any too economical in its expenditure of coal. The supplies of oil and gas are also limited, and prices very high.
Our remaining source of energy, then, is water-power. The people of the United States are not unmindful of this, for every state in the Union is to-day doing everything it can to develop its internal water-powers with a view to conserving the coal supply of the whole country. The municipalities in the province of Ontario have also done for themselves a splendid work in this respect, and have saved the people of Ontario millions in their combined water-power scheme. For some years the Niagara river was looked upon as one of the greatest scenic wonders of

the world and wTas famous chiefly for its beautiful Horseshoe falls, its small Maid of the Mist, and its rainbow. But a new day and a new era dawned when science discovered the power inherent in falling water-a discovery that has conferred a boon on every man, woman, and child in Ontario, and has been the cause of the greatest industrial expansion in that district that has ever been known in the history of Canada. I have here plates and photographs of some forty companies which have located in the Niagara district as the result of science doing what it did to develop Niagara water-power. In commercial and domestic lighting, this power development has saved my own city $22,000,00ft since 1911. This book contains a list of the manufacturing concerns, cement, chemical, paper, electric and metal companies of all kinds, foundries, motor car companies, and those engaged in manufacturing by-products, that have been established in the Niagara peninsula as the result of cheap light and power. Just look at the great basic industries that have sprung up in that district, and we had not one of them before the development of Niagara water-power. What has happened in the Niagara district yesterday and to-day will occur along the St. Lawrence if this Parliament has the courage and vision which I hope it has to carry out this work.
To sum up some of the arguments in favour of this work, those who support this canal argue that not only can the power be produced cheaply and command a ready sale, but that it will pay the bulk of the cost of the improvement. The canal can be linked up with the superpower scheme on the Atlantic coast serving the territory from the 39th parallel, near Washington, D.C., to the 44th parallel, 22 miles north of Portland, Me., and from there to the river St. Lawrence. The St. Lawrence will also be linked up on the Canadian side with a great Canadian superpower scheme, consisting of the HydroElectric system in Ontario, and the Ottawa river and part of Quebec, and can supply also power for the electrification of federal railways from Quebec to Fort William.
Now this work will conserve the coal supply. It is figured that three out of every five tons of coal consumed by a railway locomotive is an economic waste, that the present system of steam locomotion is a wasteful and not an economical system. Evidence to that eifect appears in a report which is before this House to-day.

St. Lawrence Waterway
The construction of this great waterway will relieve the railways of the burden of carrying millions of tons of coal and will effect a most decided economy. Markets for the consumption of the power to be developed will be created along the St. Lawrence. Cheap light and power will be available and this waterway will become the scene of the greatest industrial expansion in the history of Canada or of the North American continent. Small towns like Three Rivers, Brockville, Kingston, Coburg and others will grow enormously, and their population will be tremendously increased. Not only that but entirely new communities will spring into existence and this spectacle of prosperity will be witnessed all the way up to the head of the Great Lakes. The unemployment situation will be automatically solved: there will be an abundance of work for all. The St. Lawrence route, just as the Niagara river is to-day, will witness the establishment of basic plants of all kinds including chemical companies, iron and steel found-aries, paper companies, motor companies, by product concerns and production plants of all descriptions; and if the people of Canada will only have the same courage and faith in this scheme as the people of Ontario had in the development of the Niagara district, we shall witness wonderful industrial developments in connection with this great project. Let me read a few words from a statement made by Colonel John Finnie one of the greatest electrical engineers on the continent, a gentleman of international reputation, before the Conservation Commission of the United States regarding this question:
X believe that the water-power of the St. Lawrence is infinitely more value to commerce than any navigation which will use the streams after they have been improved for navigation. But most fortunately, there is no conflict between the two because any proper development of the St. Lawrence for power will at the same time take care of the navigation features. He held that the value of this power would be sufficient to carry the cost of the entire undertaking with navigation and power; that the rates would be reasonable. There was no question as to the possibility of marketing as all the available power on the St. Lawrence could be readily absorbed by growing industries. Col. Finney described the projected superpower line, a high tension transmission line designated to serve the Atlantic sea Board from Maine to Virginia, which will always be the workshop of America, and with the .proposed superpower line in Ontario, Quebec and the Ottawa river, each country would have a superpower zone to distribute its alloted share and these would be a great industrial revival on both sides of the St. Lawrence.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word or two about the financial side of this question because some objection to the project has been raised by the financial interests of Montreal. The same objection was raised when the power development scheme in the Niagara district was launched in 1905. I remember well, when the late Sir James Whitney and Sir Adam Beck proposed the undertaking of the Hydro Electric system from which 374 municipalities derive power to-day and have made such a gigantic success of, the opponents of the scheme bestowed upon its promoters the title of "amateur anarchists". You all know what a magnificent success that system has proved; yet if the promoters of that scheme had been influenced by the doubts and fears and lack of courage which characterize some people who are opposing this great waterway project to-day we should never have witnessed any such hydro-electrical power movement in the province of Ontario, and that province would never have been able to take care, as it did, of the munition plants which manufactured munitions during the war. At one time during that great struggle Sir Henry Drayton, then Chairman of the Railway Commission but later Finance Minister of Canada and now an honoured member of this House, pointed out that Ontario was supplying at one period nearly one-third of the munitions needed for our men at the front. But for the carrying out of the hydro-electric scheme Ontario would not have had the power which enabled it to render such great war assistance to the Empire. At that time also there happened to be a shortage of coal, and what a terrible condition of aifairs it would have been only for the Hydro, as there was even then a lack of power as well. As it was owing to lack of power during the war, many industries in Ontario had to close down and hundreds of men were turned out of work through no fault of their own. If we have the same faith and courage now as the men of 1905 displayed in connection with the Hydro Electric development the present project will be boldly taken up with the result that the revenue from the power developed will be more than sufficient to meet the cost of the work.
Let me mention another interesting feature in connection with power development. The privately-owned power companies in the Niagara district, representing " an investment of $32,000,000, are now being taken over by the city of Toronto and the
St. Lawrence Waterway

Hydro-Electric Commission. This will result in the establishment of public ownership throughout the entire Niagara power zone on the Canadian side and will avoid the evils of duplication. Lack of vision is by no means an uncommon thing in our public men. The late Hon. Alexander Mackenzie had some doubts about the building of the Canadian Pacific railway. He argued that it would be better to tear the rails up and store them at Port Arthur rather than to construct a railway to the coast which would be a colossal failure. Let me read a few lines from what he said on one occasion:
It would he better to pile the rails up at Port Arthur and leave them unused rather than lay two streaks of rust to the Pacific Coast.
Now, any one who had been rash enough in his day to predict that in the year 1920, such a volume as 335,000,000 bushels of grain would be taken out from the West would have been deemed a lunatic away back in 1874 or 1878.
In other countries vision and courage have been displayed in dealing with questions of this kind. Take the deepening of the canal at Frankfort in Germany; take the building of the great ship-canal from Manchester to the sea, the latter a deep waterway 35 miles long and 450 feet wide. Manchester was dead commercially in the year 1880. There were in that city 5,000 vacant houses and 200 factories closed down-actually the place was stagnant. To-day as the result of the building of that canal it is the third largest shipping port in England. Liverpool fought the deepening of that canal as likely to injure Liverpool and then built the docks on the Mersey, but it was the best thing which ever happened for that city. Liverpool will acknowledge that to-day although it fought the project for many years. Some of the financial interests in the city of Montreal look upon the present project in somewhat the same light that Liverpool once did the Manchester ship-canal. Let me say that I am a member of the Port Authorities Association. There should be no sectional jealousy in an enterprise of this kind. Toronto itself feels that what will help to develop the ports of the province of Quebec and the maritime provinces and the Pacific coast will be for the good of Toronto as well. There may be some differences of opinion about the St. Lawrence waterway project, but I plead with 'the opponents of this measure not to hold up Montreal to-day as opposed to this work. There has been a change in the

sentiment in Montreal from that which prevailed three or four years ago. I have been told by one of the Montreal Harbour Commission that they are not opposed to the construction of this canal and have not passed any resolution in regard to it- they have an open mind with respect to the project. The stand taken to-day by the financial interests in Montreal is that they do not oppose the deepening of the canal, but they say that when the ships from the West come to the port of Montreal the cargoes from the head of the lakes will have to be transhipped to larger vessels in that port for conveyance overseas, In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, that argument is futile when we bear in mind the attitude of Montreal at the time the ship-canal between that city and Quebec was undertaken. The idea then was to make Montreal the terminus instead of the ancient city of Quebec, and no such objection was raised at that time by Quebec. They never thought that by taking it to the port of Montreal they would be transferring most of the business from Quebec to Montreal. If that were true, the port of Montreal is no more an inland port than Windsor. It is an inland port built up by deep water channels at the expense of the people of iCanada, and we say the inland deep water channels should be extended to the head of the lakes in the interests of the people of this country, and in the interests of navigation. Opposition to the project also developed at the Montreal hearing of the commission and again it is the interests of Montreal against the country at large. The arguments advanced at Montreal, however, were of a somewhat different nature than those of New York state, the contention being that while the St. Lawrence should be deepened and made suitable for vessels of large capacity between the great lakes and Montreal, they should not proceed further than that city but transfer "their cargoes to ocean vessels" at Montreal; * also that it would not pay ocean ships to make the passage up the lakes.
That may be Montreal's view of the matter, but they will not find many who will agree with them. When it was decided to bring ocean vessels to Montreal and make it the terminus for ocean trade instead of the ancient city of Quebec, Montreal had no objections to offer on the ground that by so doing it might injure the city of Quebec, and they have as little right non/ to object to ocean ships passing Montreal and proceeding further. At one time the maxi-

St. Lawrence Watenvay
mum depth between Quebec and Montreal was only twelve feet, but by continuous dredging we now have a channel thirty-five feet deep and 600 feet wide through lake St. Peter.
I am surprised at the stand taken by the Premier of Quebec, Mr. Taschereau, whom I looked upon as a very capable and progressive public man. I may say that, like his predecessor, he has done a great deal for Quebec in building good roads, in erecting court houses for the municipalities, registry offices, lands titles offices, and other provincial buildings, which in Quebec are built by the province. I commend him for doing that. I believe he has done a great deal in the way of promoting good legislation. I do not agree with him in a great many ways but I appreciate what he has done in that line. He is considering the problem from a local and a provincial standpoint. What he says regarding the erection of a dam and power house on the American side is not confirmed by the report of the Deep Waterways Commission, which takes the opposite stand. This site for the dam and power house will have to be selected later by agreement. In another part of his statement he says, "We want to see the interests of Quebec protected." But the interests of Ontario are not going to be sacrificed, with 700,000 horse-power belonging to Ontario. Why should Ontario sacrifice part of this power because Quebec will not let us have it?
I would like for about five minutes to sum up some of the important advantages of this canal, and to cite some of the evidence I gave before the Deep Waterways Commission. I will read a few paragraphs. The first paragraph I will read says:
The advantages of the St. Lawrence route.
(1)	It is one of the great natural waterways of the world.
(2)	The cost of improvement is less than other routes moreover it would he divided between the two nations sharing its benefits.
It is a high speed highway avoiding long passages.
Eighty per cent of the vessels used on the Suez canal are not more than 25 feet draught. If we insist on an all Canadian route we are going to have a rival American route and both of them will not be successful. I believe there will be a distinct advantage in joining hands with the United States in this work. Millions of horse-power are available incidental to the project. This development would represent a saving of coal running into millions of tons annually. Coal miners may go on
strike, but the St. Lawrence never goes on strike. This freight development is a byproduct incidentally of carrying out this work. Nature has provided this flowing route to the sea for two reasons. For a great waterway to the sea, and for a great power plant for the development of Canadian commerce. The fact that this work is feasible is proven by what happened in 1911 before the Rivers and Harbours Committee at Washington, where they stated that they were willing to deepen the river to a depth of 30 feet for the privilege of obtaining that water-power. Every year
4,000,000 horse-power of electric energy is going to waste in the St. Lawrence; the equivalent of $800,000 worth of coal is being wasted every year, and the finest system of inland waterways is lying idle because deep-draught vessels cannot pass forty-six miles of the St. Lawrence river on their way to the upper lakes.
The St. Lawrence ranks with the Suez and Panama canals in its magnitude and importance. To provide for a continuous deep waterway, 2,300 miles from the head of the lakes to tidewater, 46 miles of the St. Lawrence would have to be made passable. The cost will be $250,000,000 as I stated in my evidence, but I think it will be found by the report that the cost would be $270,000,000.
We have choked railway facilities in Canada with the high freight rates and cost of transportation, equal on an average to 20 per cent of the value of the goods to be transported, with also a shortage of coal. People are demanding that use be made of the waterways, deeper canals and the use of the millions of horse-power unused and available. The only opposition is in New York and Montreal. Montreal is opposed for local reasons as distinguished from national reasons. They are looking for a larger Montreal. They will readily secure one from this canal. Canada and the United States are not as much interested in the local aims and objects of this place and that as in furnishing the necessities to the great bulk of the people as cheaply as possible. Montreal is no more a sea port than Toronto or Fort William. It is an inland port made an ocean port because of deep river channels. We say these should be extended to the head of the lakes. Montreal's other plea is that it is not practical. Some people said the same thing about all the hydro development and the deepening of the Welland, but eminent engineers in the United States and Canada say it is practical. Canada and the United

St. Lawrence Waterway

States are all bottled up because of lack of an outlet to the sea, although both produce vast amounts of all the necessities of life, far more than we can use at home. They have no adequate outlet, with the result that much of our production goes to waste. I may instance the way fruit and vegetables in the Niagara district have gone to waste every fall for lack of transportation.
The great bulk of the developed power will belong to Canada. Some say Canada will want to take it all. Not so, Canada raises wheat and other agricultural products and sells them abroad and will also do the same with part of this power. The Dominion will not monopolize the power of the St. Lawrence. What Canada needs also is with this canal a forward national shipbuilding policy that would have Canadian ships go out on to seven seas and bring trade to Canada up the St. Lawrence to the head of the Great lakes. Nature has carved out a great highway from the lakes to the gulf of St. Lawrence on the east and to the gulf of Mexico on the south, both routes offering a downhill haul. To Canada and to the great nation that built the Panama canal this should prove an easy task. Had Europe such an opportunity, the project would have been completed and progressively improved for a thousand years or more. China did this more than three thousand years ago. Our great inland seas must be connected to the east with salt water. To the south, to the United States, the Mississippi offers her one logical channel. To the east, and I say it with equal confidence, the St. Lawrence offers the one logical channel to Canada and the United States in unison. The natural route, by the St. Lawrence, is already made for us, except for some forty-six odd miles obstructed by rapids. Overcome this obstruction and there is clear sailing all the way to the sea. It is a national duty-a Canadian duty-an international duty to develop water-power wherever possible. Give us this mighty co-labourer with coal in keeping the wheels of industry revolving and you will put the country beyond the power of any man or group of men to cripple and imperil as the country is crippled and imperiled to-day. It is the shortest by some hundreds of miles from any of the lake ports to Liverpool or northern Europe and the Mediterranean, as will be seen by the following.
From Chicago to Christiana by way of New York is 5,767 miles; from Chicago to Christiana by the St. Lawrence is 4,927

miles-a big difference. The St. Lawrence is also much shorter to Liverpool than New York. To the Mediterranean also the way is shorter by the St. Lawrence than by New York. And is shorter also- to Italy, Greece, the Black sea, and India by the Suez. Now distance is not everything, but in this case it means *both time and money. Improvements of the St. Lawrence route will not in any way lessen the value of other waterways which are regarded by some as rival routes.
We have engineering and commercial assurance of these three facts:
(1)	It can be done; it is practical.
(2)	The cost would be less than other routes proposed.
(3)	There would be developed water
power running into millions of tons of coal per annum and millions of horse power available for trade and commerce and industrial development. I believe that one joint route for Canada and the United States is better than two rival routes. I believe that such a route can be accomplished more cheaply, that it provides a more direct way to the markets of Europe, that it is more practicable, more serviceable, better than any other plan yet offered. I believe that this improved St Lawrence will bring great commercial development to our own country and corresponding benefit to the people of the world with whom we shall trade. The St. Lawrence route has long appealed to my interest. I was hopeful, and at last 'we have got a report which gives us in concrete form the cost and the possibilities that will grow out of this great international waterway. The water has been running to waste through all the ages.	[DOT]
The United States spent something over $400,000,000 to construct the Panama canal, but as far as serving the business interests of that country and the world are concerned, the benefits are not comparable to those that would come, through the development of the St. Lawrence waterway to the sea, to Canada, the United States and the world. One objector in the United States said that the canal is to be built in conjunction with Canada. The waterway is for some distance the natural boundary between these two countries. Both nations are equally interested in its development. It is big enough to accommodate both countries. These countries live in amity together, and this great improvement would benefit both. Canada has expended $95,000,000 in improvements in the St. Lawrence river and she has voted


St. Lawrence Waterway
$55,000,000 for improvements in the Welland canal. She should have a route to the sea for her vessels, and this project is the least expensive that makes for an ocean waterway. It has within its development to pay for its own expenses, and no one will deny that, because practical engineers have made the demonstration of what is possible. The idea that the people of the two countries own a waterway one thousand miles in length, reaching into the heart of a continent which is the greatest in production and consuming power in the world,a channel of still water, running to the ocean, and do not provide proper access for it, especially when that project promises to be self-sustaining from its power development alone-seems to me to speak such a lack of courage on the part of our people that I cannot believe it is true. Increased facilities of transportation to meet the ever enlarging demands of distribution can only be provided through the improvement and utilization of our waterways and aiding water borne traffic. Navigable waterways are intended primarily for commerce; and the expenditure of public moneys can only be justified when they are to be so used.
Speaking as a Toronto Harbour Commissioner of twenty years practical experi->
ence, I believe that eighty per cent of the present ocean-going craft can reach the upper lakes by the present channels when the way is opened through the St. Lawrence and the new Welland. More than ninety-six per cent can reach lake Erie by the same improvement. In seeking a route to the Atlantic, we must have the best highway that can be obtained.
I have heard at the various conventions of the port authorities of the world which I have attended some arguments against this project; they were more fancied than real and sectional rather than national. Let us consider this question from a national standpoint-not the narrow, local parish point of view-and thereby do the greatest good to the greatest number. I have noted some of the objections and give them here, with the answer to each:
(1)	It would be an economic failure and
waste of public money. Answer:	The
power incidental will pay for the work.
(2)	The cost would be prohibitive. Answer: The deep waterway reports say that it would not.
(3)	Fogs and ice make the St. Lawrence route too hazardous. It is all right for six or seven months. Answer: The
fogs and ice on the Atlantic play havoc with the steamship service there as well.
(4)	Ocean vessels cannot navigate in the restricted channels nor afford the delays of lockage in canals. Answer: This objection is not sound, the report says so.
(5)	There will be no return tonnage, and one-way traffic cannot be developed. Answer: The west is a great consumer.
(6)	The purpose is to enable Canada to control the export grain trade. Answer: That is not so.
(7)	It is designed to destroy the competition of the barge canal. Answer: It would cater to a different form of trade, and would be a feeder to the barge canal.
(8)	The power is not needed. Answer: It will soon be badly needed in Canada and especially in the United States.
(9)	It would expose the United States to the peril of invasion by Great Britain. Answer: The British fleet has been for six centuries the defender and protector of civilization. It saved civilization and liberty in the days of Philip of Spain, Louis XIV, Napoleon and the Kaiser. Only for the British fleet in the years from 1914 to 1918, we would have had the awful horror of the German war on our own soil, in Montreal, Quebec, Toronto, Boston, New York and Chicago. The British fleet saved America's shores. There is no danger of the invasion of the Great Lakes. The hope of the peace of the world is in amity between England and America.
We talk about disarmament. The case of the Great Lakes is a shining example to the world of what can be done by two nations in this regard. What could be more significant of the spirit that inspired the Disarmament conference than the simple fact that from the river St. Lawrence to the head of the Great Lakes there is not to-day any sign of a single armed vessel or armed fort? It shows that two peoples, with the same ideals and aspirations, can live side by side in friendly relations without any resort to works of defence.
Before I conclude I desire to read three of four paragraphs from the report now before me of the International Joint Commission, appointed by both governments. That commission was given certain instructions and it submitted answers to nine questions asked them. I shall not read the questions; I shall leave that duty to some other hon. member. The questions, as do the answers, speak for themselves. Having considered the question from every economic standpoint, and having heard

St. Lawrence Waterway

numerous witnesses, the commission have now brought in a report strongly in favour of the proposed work, from the navigation, the power, and the financial standpoints. The report states that an analysis submitted before the commission made it clear that the consensus of opinion of the two countries, as revealed in the public hearing, was on the whole distinctly favourable to the improvement of the St. Lawrence. There are two or three sentences I wish to read:
The opposition to the suggested improvement centred largely in the State of New York, but was also supported by representatives of various public bodies in New England and in some of the Atlantic Coast States south of New York as well as in the City of Montreal.
But the few Canadians who opposed it did so because they favoured a rural route. P. 156. Further on, the report says:
The Commission is inclined to the view that the St. .Lawrence route would afford a material saving in transportation rates over any of the existing routes between points in the territory economically tributary to the St. Lawrence and overseas points.
The report refers to the time factor as follows (P. 161) :
The Commission is of the opinion that losses of time-due to delay in locks and restricted speed in canals and river channels would not prove a serious obstacle to the use of the proposed route-by ocean-going vessels.
At page 166 the report says that there is nothing in the evidence to warrant the belief that ocean-going vessels could not safely navigate the waters of the St. Lawrence river, and further on it states:
The terms of the reference make it clear, in the opinion of the commission, that the intention of the two Governments was that the proposed improvement of the Upper St. Lawrence should serve primarily the interests of navigation and commerce and only incidentally those of water power.
In answer to the statement made by Mr. Taschereau and others that the matter was being really engineered by the American water-power interests to serve their own ends, the commission has this to say:
The Commission is confident that there is no justification whatever for these assertions.
As a matter of fact, public attention, as I have pointed out is centered on the question from the point of view of the general improvement afforded in transportation, navigation and powers, and the economic advantage to Canada.
Now, this is the most important question this Parliament will have to deal with, and I would ask hon. members on all sides to approach the consideration of it with an
[Mr Church.]
open mind. Do not let us consider only from the sectional point what is good for Montreal, or Toronto, or Quebec, or any other single section; let us consider what is good in the national interests and that of the whole country, in order that we may obtain some relief from the heavy freight charges and solve our transportation problems aright. I submit that action is necessary in this matter for several reasons: to develop our water-power and improve our traffic; to solve the unemployment question; to develop the great interior of this country and particularly the great West which is suffering to such an extent to-day; and generally to make 'Canada a better place "for our war heroes to live in." As things are many of our unfit soldiers are out of work in many large centres of population to-day, going about seeking charity in the larger centres of population. This canal would do more to solve the unemployment problem than any other agency, and I urge the Prime Minister to take steps in the matter immediately. The question was considered of sufficient importance in the United States to justify six weeks' discussion in the two houses of Parliament there, and the committees. It has been made a football long enough by legislators, and I think it is time for the Parliament of Canada to do something practical. We have had a number of minor questions discussed in this House. On Monday afternoon and evening, for example, we had under discussion an academic question which, though important, was of trivial concern to the people of this country as compared with the question we are now considering. That discussion on Monday was no doubt interesting from an academic point of view, but this subject transcends in importance any of the minor questions that we have been debating. I do urge the Government, the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen), the Progressives, and all parties to get together and so arrange matters that all those who desire to speak on this question might have ample opportunity to put their views before the House. For, I repeat, this is the greatest question this Parliament will have to settle, and one of the greatest questions since Confederation. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I desire to thank yourself and the hon. members of this House for the courteous hearing and attention that has been given me. As I said, I could only begin to touch the fringe of this great and intricate problem in the very short time at my disposal. I have,

St. Lawrence Watenvay
however, dealt with the most salient points affecting the economic, the transportation, the navigation, the power and light, the unemployment, the shipbuilding, the rates and tolls, and the financial sides of this big question.

I had not anticipated the honour of taking part at an early stage in this debate, but I feel that if we may congratulate the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) on bringing this very momentous question to the attention of the House, some endeavour should be made at once to place before hon. members the other side of the case. The hon. member in a very able, although not very comprehensive speech, has presented his own side of the question; and, while it is not my intention to try to follow him in every step that he has taken, I shall attempt to sum up in a general way the arguments on the side of the case which my hon,. friend has not put before us. I want to remind the House also of some of the very good reasons which have been advanced why the Government should be very cautious in this matter, should approach the whole question warily, and, in fact, should refrain at the present time from taking the least practical action. If the flow of the St. Lawrence was as abundant and tumultuous as the faculty of speech of my hon. friend (Mr. Church), we might take chances with it, but in my view the St. Lawrence is too precious an asset to this country for us to lightly and without the strongest motives either attempt to alter its navigability, or enter into partnership with another country in regard to it, or place a mortgage on our property rights in it.
It has been pointed out, and very properly, that the deepening of the St. Lawrence river to permit ocean vessels to reach the Great Lakes is no more than an engineering problem. I grant, Mr. Speaker, that, given the money, it is possible for engineers to provide a twenty-five or even a thirty-foot channel from Montreal to the Great Lakes. But that is not the point. There is a financial and also an international side to this question. Can Canada bear her share of the cost of this undertaking? That is one point. Further, will the results expected warrant the expenditure? That is another point. But a more important point than either seems to me to be this: Is it desirable to enter into a partnership of this kind with the United States?
As to the cost, the situation is very obscure. We have not any precise data as to what this great enterprise would cost. It has been reported that a twenty-five-foot waterway can be constructed for $250,000,000. But it has also been pointed out that this estimate does not cover the deepening of the lake harbours, of the channels of the Great Lakes, nor of the connecting rivers. In this connection I need not remind this House that every time an enterprise of this kind is launched in Parliament the estimated cost is always very much lower than the actual cost of construction.
But the point of my argument this afternoon is not directed so much against this scheme as to show that we do not have enough information at the present time to warrant us entering into it. As to the cost, I would point out from the International Joint Commission's report on this St. Lawrence waterway, which was distributed to us at the beginning of the session, that it is rather dubious what the cost will be. From the summary of conclusions on page 178 I quote the following paragraph:
The whole question of the distribution of cost has given the commission some concern.
May I interject that it should give us even more concern?
If the area to be benefited were all in one country, the problem of financing the improvement would be a comparatively simple one, but as the matter stands the situation is complicated not merely by the fact that two neighbouring countries are joining in the project, but that these countries are unequal in population, unequal in wealth, unequal in their ability to make effective use of the waterway. That is the situation to-day, but it does not necessarily follow that it will always be the situation.
On the same page this matter of cost is further discussed and I read:
Objection may be made that the proposed principle of dividing the cost in .proportion to the benefits each country derives from the improvement could hardly be put into effect until the works had been completed and In operation for a sufficient period to secure reliable data on the subject.
Again on the same page the commissioners state:
In other words, each country should be debited with its share of the entire cost of all works necessary for navigation, including the cost of the Welland ship canal, based upon the proportion the cargo tonnage carried to and from its own ports by way of the St. Lawrence bears to the entire tonnage by the same route. The ratio to be charged to each obviously would require to be readjusted periodically.
I think, Mr. Speaker, I have quoted sufficiently from the report of the commission to show that there is no precise in-

St. Lawrence Waterway
formation as to what this scheme would cost Canada, and to show that we would he altogether in the hands of our powerful partner to the south as to what proportion of the cost should he assessed to us.
The estimate that this waterway would cost $250,000,000 is certainly much below the actual cost. But even if we accept that as a correct estimate, and assume that we would be responsible for one-half of it, I submit that in the present state of our finances it would be very unwise indeed to add to our obligations to that extent.
As to improving the navigability of the St. Lawrence, there is a lurking suspicion that this is only the ostensible purpose, and that the real purpose of the promoters is to promote water-power.
But, in objecting to this scheme generally, Mr. Speaker, I would point out that I am not offering the profane opinion of a mere city member, but that I am rather summarizing the arguments that have been advanced against it by men whose opinion is authoritative and deserves great respect. The effect of those arguments is that it is not at all evident that there would be any improvement in navigation as a result of carrying out this scheme at all commensurate with the expenditure involved. You are aware, Mr. Speaker, that deep sea vessels cannot compete with lake vessels because the latter have three times the cargo capacity for the corresponding draught; also the deep sea vessel has to be built more strongly and costs three times as much per ton as does the lake vessel. Therefore the claim that ocean vessels could come up the river to our inland ports in competition with our lake vessels is indeed one that is very much open to question.
I think we may reasonably come to the conclusion that while many of the experts have pronounced on the feasibility of a deep waterway of this kind, and that it might bring lake vessels to Montreal, yet it would not at all enable the ocean vessels to profitably proceed to the head of the lakes. In other words, the truth about this water navigation from the middle west to the ocean is that it would require two, and possibly three kinds of craft to complete it. First, it would require the lake vessels proper, built light and inexpensively for cargo-carrying purposes exclusively; then barges to traverse the intervening areas between the lakes and the seaports, and, finally, the heavy and costly sea vessels with large crews, staunchly

built, requiring expensive insurance, to carry the cargo the rest of the way. But, Mr. Speaker, we have strong suspicion, as I have said, that the navigation side of the project is only an accessory feature; that the water-power project is the essential motive that has inspired the promoters of the scheme. I quote in support of this contention the New York Times. Of course, it will be argued that New York stands very much with Montreal on this matter, but as I have said, I am merely placing before the House the argument-on our side. The New York Times says:
The people of New York, under our constitution, own the lands under water along the St. Lawrence valley. No one has suggested a way to compensate these owners if their land is condemned. And condemnation proceedings, under the federal statutes, may he brought only where the rights condemned are to be used for navigational purposes. Hence the camouflage of benefiting navigation.
As for Canada, it has been submitted that we have in this country water-power possibilities much greater than we employ at the present time, and that if this scheme would give the United States a vast amount of water-power which they need, it would be practically using Canadian resources to supply them with that water-power, while we on this side would only sacrifice our right to those resources without any compensating benefit. But the main argument and the main objection to this project, Mr. Speaker, is that it would involve an international partnership with a very powerful neighbour, a neighbour whom we expect to exact the letter as well as the spirit of all contracts; and it would give rise to innumerable conflicts in the future. We know that we have been at peace with the United States for a long while, but we also know by experience that every time there has been a dispute we have bought peace, sometimes dearly, by sacrificing our part of the bargain. Need I remind the House that on the occasion of the Maine boundary controversy Canada maintained peace only by sacrificing a portion of territory which should be included in the province of Quebec and which now forms a very wealthy and prosperous part of the United States? Need I remind the House that when the question of the Alaskan boundary was discussed, again we had to buy peace by sacrificing what we thought was our property in that part of the country?
The other day the member for West-mount-St. Henri (Mr. Mercier) brought to the attention of the House a despatch to the effect that the United States repre-

St. Lawrence Waterway
sentatives were already discussing this matter with the British Embassy at Washington. I say in all confidence, Mr. Speaker, that I do not believe the British Embassy has gone into this matter with the American representatives; but I do not think I am far from the truth when I say that if the British Embassy had been disposed to do so, the American representatives would have been only too glad to settle this matter over our heads. Anyway, if we are to judge by editorials and articles in the American press with regard to this matter, we can well make up our minds that this partnership, as I say, would be very dangerous to our own side of the bargain. I do not wish to quote at length; I realize that, especially on Wednesday, when we have to adjourn at six o'clock, it is only fair that I should give as much time as possible to other members who desire to speak on the subject. But I would like to place on Hansard a couple of quotations on this matter of partnership. The first is from the report of the New York State Commission. It reads thus-I will quote only one paragraph:
For a hundred years the two nations have been in perfect accord and no thoughtful person would suggest that these cordial relations should ever be severed, but as a matter of prudence and good statesmanship, if a ship canal were ever to be built down the St. Lawrence river, and for nine-tenths of the distance from Lake Ontario to the gulf of St. Lawrence wholly within Canadian territory and under the sovereign control of the Dominion of Canada, if not the British Empire, then there should be a cession of territory the entire length of the St. Lawrence river, five or ten miles back from the river, constituting a zone like the Panama Canal Zone, secured by treaty with the Republic of Panama.
I would like also to quote again from the report of the International Joint Commission, to show you, Mr. Speaker, that this partnership with the United States would involve innumerable causes for passible conflicts. I quote again from the conclusions of the report; and I would like to point out that I should at least be given some credit for taking my arguments from the very report which is supposed to support this scheme. The report says, on page 179:
In regard to the method of control, the commission is conscious of the fact that the peculiar character of the St. Lawrence, partly international and partly national, creates an unusual situation, and it believes that, in order to combine the fullest possible liberty of action on the part of each country in its own territory, with the efficient co-ordination of the several parts of the completed improvement, all "navigation works'' lying wholly within one country and capable of economic and efficient administration
as complete and independent units, should be maintained and operated by the country in
which they are located-
Nobody can find fault with that, so far.
-that "navigation works" not lying wholly within one country and not capable of economic and efficient administration as complete and independent units, should be maintained and operated by an international board on which each country would have equal representation; and that this board should also have the right of inspection of those "navigation works."
I admit it is proposed that we should have equal representation on that board, but who will pretend for one moment that even if numerically we have the same representation as the United States on a board of that kind, the representatives of Canada, able as they might be, powerful as they might be in their own country, can ever counter-balance the influence of the representatives of the United States if an important conflict should arise regarding those works which are of a national character?
Further, as part of the recommendations of the commission, found on page 181 of this report, it is said:
5. That, assuming the adoption of the plans of the engineering board, or of other plans also involving a readjustment of the international boundary, in order to bring each of the power houses on its own side of the boundary, appropriate steps be taken to transfer from one country or the other, as the case may be, the slight acreage of submerged land Involved.
Again I submit, that over this one little paragraph in the recommendations of the commision an important and involved discussion could take place over what they call the slight acreage of our territory, and if we entered into a discussion of that matter, we do not know where it would end. I might also quote paragraphs 7 and 8 of these recommendations to show that in more than one respect there could be discussion between the two countries on matters of territory, on navigation, on the distribution of water power, and in every case we would be in the position of being the much weaker and the much smaller nation discussing these matters with a very powerful neighbour who could practically get from us all that it demanded. I shall say no more for the reason that I gave only a moment ago. I would like to hear from the House on this question. I do not say that the House should condemn altogether this enterprise, but I think it will agree with me that there are grave doubts on the different aspects of this project, as to its cost, as to its value for navigation purposes, and for the international develop-
St. Lawrence Waterway

ment of power, and finally as to the political consequence of such a partnership -with the United States of America. The report makes it very clear that the commission itself did not reach a definite conclusion, for at page 180 I find this:
The commission believes that, before any particular scheme is finally adopted, all the available engineering data, including the report and plans of the engineering board and all comments thereon or alternative plans, should be referred to a special technical board for careful consideration and report.
And paragraph 4, on the next page:
That there shall be an exhaustive investigation of the extent and character of the damage through flowage involved in the plan of development finally adopted.
These paragraphs show amply that the commission themselves feel that before they arrive at a conclusion, they should get the two countries together once more and make a further investigation, and that even this report, which is supposed to favour the scheme, is not at all definite in it's conclusions. These doubts are sufficient, in my mind, to lead the Canadian Government to exercise the strictest caution.
It rests with the promoters of the project to create and instill the strongest conviction, if they ever hope to have it carried out. But for those who do object to it, it is sufficient to point out the dubious, questionable, and altogether obscure character of the whole enterprise. Only the strongest evidence could bear out the project. This does not exist even in this report. I think we have shown, on the contrary, that the project coasts along dangers and threats, both economic and national, at every turn and winding of its course. I therefore would urge the Government and the House not to accept this resolution.

Mr. Speaker, I just wish to speak for a few minutes on this matter, to protest against acceding to the request of the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) that another day be set apart for the discussion of this resolution.
I am not going to discuss whether the project is feasible or not, but if we spend the time of the House in discussing questions like this, which are not pressing at the present time and, indeed, are not to be thought of, very important and urgent questions will have to be compressed into a very small space at the end of the session or not dealt with at all. There is no doubt in my mind that if this project

is carried out, the estimated cost of $250,000,000 will be doubled by the time it is completed.
What is the situation? I do not want to deal at any great length with western conditions. I think those have been stressed sufficiently for the House to realize the seriousness of the situation. I shall just mention one incident in order to give point to what has already been said. Two days before I left my home, the man who rents my farm said to me, " I can go out now and buy oats for less than it costs to thresh mine." Farmers at the present time are in need of help to buy seed. There are very many urgent matters for which we need money, and I think that is sufficient reason for me to arrive at the conclusion at once that the idea of starting on this project of deepening the St. Lawrence river and the Welland canal so that ocean vessels may go up to Fort William, while it may be quite practicable in the future, and I think will be, at the present time is simply out of the question. That being the case, if another day is set apart for its discussion, where will we be?
I came here with a very good impression of Parliament, and since I have been sitting here, that impression has not lessened; I think as much of Parliament today as I did when I arrived. But I have found what I expected, that occasionally a great deal of time is wasted. I have attended large conventions enough to know that it is impossible to prevent that. I have arrived at the conclusion that there are some cities in this country that are rather expensive. Judging from the pages that are put on Hansard by the representatives from Toronto, I fancy that Toronto is rather an expensive city. One argument made in favour of this project was that it was going to build up small cities into larger ones, and, I suppose, make the large ones still larger. I believe that the attitude of this party in the House is sometimes misunderstood. We have been charged with being narrowminded and with not being able to see other interests besides our own. I wish to make it plain just what our attitude is with regard to these matters. When it comes to a question of developing a great industry which, when developed, will cause life to flow through the channels of trade throughout the whole country, you will find us very, very generous. That includes such works as agriculture, fisheries, and the development of our mines and forests. But I submit that when money is poured out freely into the

St. Lawrence Waterway
large cities it works in very narrow channels and in very small circles, and it is a question to my mind whether this country would be any better off in any respect if Toronto, or Montreal, or Hamilton were doubled in size to-morrow. It is just a question if it would not prove a greater burden on the country at large, than a benefit. The cities are overgrown now; in comparison with the country, they are over-developed. Therefore, I think the policy of Canada at the present time and for some few years to come should be to decentralize, to cause people to go from the cities to the country, so that the country may be built up and take a position of greater relative importance as compared with the cities. That is what we need, not a policy to cause our cities to grow larger. Where does the money expended in the large cities go? It goes into the pockets of the retailers, and then into the pockets of the wholesalers and manufacturers-the movement operates in a small circle. If a city grows larger it probably helps the surrounding country within a radius of ten to twenty miles; but I cannot see that it is any great benefit to the country at large to have these urban centres grow larger than they are now. The present debate ought to be closed at six o'clock so that we shall not have to waste another day over the subject, because when the question is brought up once more, as it undoubtedly will be, the whole ground will have to be covered again.

I wish to concur in the remarks just made by the hon. member for St. James (Mr. Rin-fret) in objecting to this Parliament giving its endorsation to any scheme in which we have to enter into partnership with a foreign country. We of northern Ontario have had a waterway scheme under consideration for the last twenty-five years.. Away back in 1899 the late J. W. Poupore, then representing the county of Pontiac, advocated in this House the building of a canal entirely within the bounds of Canada-a canal to be built with Canadian capital, by Canadian labour, and controlled by the Canadian people. Therefore, when my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Church) says that all Ontario is in favour of a joint ship canal I can-on behalf of the electors of Nipissing, whom I have the honour to represent-say that we are directly opposed to the construction of the St. Lawrence deep waterway. The Georgian Bay ship canal project will meet all the requirements that the St. Lawrence deep waterway will give us, and it would confer upon Canada, western Canada in particular, all the benefits that are claimed for the latter project. The Engineering Board of the International Joint Commission have estimated that the cost of a 25 foot ship canal would be 8252,000,000. As detailed plans could not be prepared within the limited time of one year mere outline plans and lump estimates were submitted, and we are safe in concluding that these estimates will fall far short of what the real cost of this enterprise will be. Canada's initial share in the construction of this canal would be $151,000,000; and I ask hon. members who have been clamouring since this session opened for more economy and more retrenchment in expenses if this is an opportune time to add $8,000,000 in interest charges to the annual expenses of this Government. The economic advantage claimed for this scheme as far as Canada is concerned is merely the cheapen ing of the export of our north west grain by avoiding the cost of elevating at Kingston and Montreal. All other advantages favour American lake ports.
